scope.sourceTextMethod: Read every extracted full guide section, PDF144–271, from each sourcePdfPage through the page before the next control. Existing pdftotext output of the pinned PDF was read with horizontal whitespace normalized only; no source section was summarized before inspection. Two truncated output portions were reread in full (IR3.6.3/MA3.7.1 and CA3.12.1/CA3.12.2).

limitations: AI-assisted editorial comparison, not qualified human approval, certification, current applicability verification or a guarantee of 100% accuracy.
Official-host verification remains blocked/unresolved; the review uses the identified September2024 v2.13 guide snapshot.
All requested perspective fields were read; this full-field editorial pass is distinct from selected-field assessment-objective mappings and does not establish a complete instructional curriculum.
No factual correction identified means no correction identified during this bounded pass, not blanket approval. Technical jargon may still need contextual vocabulary and real learner testing.
Evidence examples are candidate materials for discussion, not exhaustive official evidence lists or proof of organizational compliance.
Current applicability has not been verified; this audit uses the pinned historical guide.

findings.issue: User reporting and communication are present, but role-appropriate incident-response training and assistance are absent from all fields although the Discussion explicitly includes them within user response. Add this teaching context without inventing a course or schedule.
findings.proposedText: Connect detection sources, responder responsibilities, containment options, recovery procedures, and user reporting into an operational workflow. Include incident-response training appropriate to each role and assistance for users responding to incidents. Preparation and analysis matter alongside the tools used during an incident.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level2 v2.13 PDF144/printed136 objective[g]; PDF145/printed137 Discussion: user-response training is linked to assigned roles and responsibilities; user-response assistance may include help desk support, assistance groups and specialist services.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

records.reviewNote: All seven incident-handling elements remain present; clarify the Discussion’s explicit role-appropriate training and assistance within user response.
Tracking, documenting, identifying internal/external recipients and notifying them remain distinct; no invented reporting deadline or universal recipients.

findings.issue: Could be read as one test at any time being enough; the guide asks about regular testing.
findings.proposedText: Examine whether the incident response capability has been tested and what the test demonstrated. This requirement does not set a specific frequency or mandate one test format, though the guide asks whether policy calls for regular testing.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 150 / printed 142 section; requirements for regular incident response plan testing

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: requirements for regular incident response plan testing

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Tests may use walkthroughs, tabletop exercises, simulations or comprehensive exercises; discussion-only exercise is not proof of every technical mechanism; no invented numeric frequency.
Hardware, software, firmware, local/nonlocal work and peripheral equipment remain in scope; maintenance is not reduced to patching.

findings.issue: Named three of the four elements and said "consider" where the requirement says "provide controls".
findings.proposedText: Keep repair work under control: control who performs maintenance and the tools, methods and mechanisms (such as automated maintenance scripts) they use. A helpful repair tool can also introduce an unwanted risk.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 154 / printed 146 section; mechanisms used to conduct system maintenance are controlled

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: mechanisms used to conduct system maintenance are controlled

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Tools, techniques, mechanisms and personnel are all addressed; diagnostic-tool approval does not substitute for personnel authorization.
Sanitization precedes off-site maintenance release, including embedded CUI-bearing storage; trusted vendor or file deletion is not substituted for sanitization.
Diagnostic/test media are checked before use; detected malicious code follows incident handling; no universal scanning product is mandated.
MFA at establishment of external nonlocal maintenance and termination afterward both retained; separate browser logout may not terminate the maintenance connection.
Workers without required authorization are supervised; temporary credentials remain controlled and the distinction from physical visitor access is preserved.

Paper and digital media both require physical control and secure storage; encryption does not replace physical accountability. The source Further Discussion’s anomalous hardcopy examples are not copied.
Authorization to access CUI on media is distinguished from knowing its storage location; physical checkout and digital restrictions are possible mechanisms.

findings.issue: Combines disposal and reuse before giving sanitize-or-destroy alternatives, which can imply destruction is an appropriate preparation for reuse. The two determination branches should be explicit in Beginner mode.
findings.proposedText: Before disposing of media containing CUI, sanitize it or destroy it. Sanitizing removes the information so it cannot be recovered. Before releasing media for reuse, sanitize it; simply deleting a file does not necessarily remove the information.
findings.sourceSupport: PDF169/printed161 objectives[a,b]: media is sanitized or destroyed before disposal; media is sanitized before release for reuse. PDF170/printed162 Further Discussion distinguishes destruction before disposal from cleaning/purging for reuse.
findings.reviewerProposedText: Before disposing of media containing CUI, sanitize or destroy it. Before releasing it for reuse, sanitize it. Removing a file from the screen does not necessarily remove the information from the media.
findings.coordinatingAdjustment: Explain sanitizing in plain language using the Discussion definition; preserve the disposal/reuse branches.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

findings.issue: Select sanitization or destruction before release leaves the destination distinction implicit. Preserve both objective branches in the technical explanation too.
findings.proposedText: Choose methods suited to the media and its destination: sanitize or destroy before disposal, and sanitize before release for reuse. Verify the result before release. Consider embedded storage in printers and network equipment, as well as familiar drives and paper records.
findings.sourceSupport: PDF169/printed161 objectives[a,b] and Discussion cover all digital and non-digital media, including scanners, copiers, printers and network components; PDF170/printed162 distinguishes disposal and reuse.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

findings.issue: The question joins sanitization or destruction with disposal or reuse, obscuring the distinction accurately stated in compliance.focus.
findings.proposedText: How is sanitization or destruction checked before disposal, and sanitization checked before release for reuse?
findings.sourceSupport: PDF169/printed161 objectives[a,b]; PDF170/printed162 Further Discussion and Potential Assessment Considerations address whether usable data remains retrievable.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

records.reviewNote: Compliance focus preserves the two objective branches, but Beginner meaning, technical focus and the second review question can imply destruction prepares media for reuse; clarify all three.

findings.issue: Moved the marking from the media to its contents; the objectives require the media itself to be marked.
findings.proposedText: A document-production process could provide appropriate templates and a review step, while a removable-media process could put a CUI label on the outside of each drive that also shows its distribution limitations, following NARA guidance.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 171 / printed 163 section; The project team labels the outside of each USB drive with an appropriate CUI label following NARA guidance

findings.proposedText: Marking templates, plus observed or appropriately redacted examples of actual marked media

records.reviewNote: Applicable CUI markings and distribution limitations are both retained; generic confidentiality labels and access enforcement are correctly distinguished from markings.

findings.issue: Limited access control to transport; objective [a] has no transport limit.
findings.proposedText: Control who can access media containing CUI. When it travels outside controlled areas, keep track of its custody: knowing who sent it is only the beginning of knowing where it went.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 173 / printed 165 section; access to media containing CUI is controlled

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: access to media containing CUI is controlled

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

findings.issue: Limited access control to transport; objective [a] has no transport limit.
findings.proposedText: Control access to CUI media, and maintain accountability throughout release, transport, and receipt. Suitable packaging, authorized handlers, transport records, and confirmation of delivery can support the process for paper or digital media.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 173 / printed 165 section; access to media containing CUI is controlled

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: access to media containing CUI is controlled

findings.issue: Asked only about transport; objective [a] covers access to CUI media generally.
findings.proposedText: Who is authorized to access CUI media, and who may handle it during transport?
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 173 / printed 165 section; Do only approved individuals have access to media containing CUI

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: Do only approved individuals have access to media containing CUI

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Access control and transport accountability include release, authorized handlers, handoffs and receipt; encryption alone is not a custody record.

findings.issue: The final clause instructs the author not to lose an exception instead of helping the learner understand the permitted alternatives.
findings.proposedText: Protect CUI stored on digital media while it is being transported. Use cryptographic protection unless alternative physical safeguards protect its confidentiality throughout the trip.
findings.sourceSupport: PDF175/printed167 requirement and objective[a] allow cryptographic mechanisms or alternative physical safeguards during transport; PDF176/printed168 Further Discussion retains alternative physical safeguarding.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

findings.issue: Read as optional. The guide says the cryptography in this requirement protects CUI and "must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11" (FIPS-validated cryptography).
findings.proposedText: Identify transported digital media and its confidentiality protection. Where cryptography protects CUI confidentiality, it must also meet SC.L2-3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography). Manage keys so the transport package does not undermine the protection.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 175 / printed 167 section; the cryptography used must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11

records.reviewNote: Cryptography or alternative physical safeguards and the digital-media transport scope are preserved; remove the author-facing instruction about not losing an exception from Beginner meaning.
Controls may be technical or procedural and restrict device classes/read-write behavior; draft correctly avoids a universal ban on all removable devices.
Identifiable owner can be an individual, organization or project; malware scanning alone does not establish ownership.

findings.issue: "Consider the applicable validation requirement" did not name it or say it is required; the guide asks whether the mechanisms are FIPS validated.
findings.proposedText: Identify backup copies and storage locations, then apply confidentiality protections appropriate to those locations. Cryptographic mechanisms or alternative physical controls can protect backups; where cryptography protects CUI, it must be FIPS-validated (SC.L2-3.13.11).
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 181 / printed 173 section; Are cryptographic mechanisms FIPS validated
findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Backup confidentiality applies at storage locations; cryptographic or alternative physical controls remain options and backup success is distinguished from confidentiality.
Screening precedes authorization, reflects role and applicable rules, and does not invent universal clearances, products or disclosure of sensitive screening details.
Protection during and after termination or extended/permanent transfer includes affected access, credentials and property; transfer actions are not forced to be identical to departure actions.
Authorization and restrictions cover systems, equipment and operating areas; technical/compliance fields retain the nonpublic-area qualification and equipment placement concerns.
Both facility and support infrastructure must be protected and monitored; public-access monitoring and wiring/power infrastructure are retained without mandating cameras.
Escorting and monitoring visitors remain separate; permanent access credential holders are distinguished from visitors, and a sign-in log alone does not demonstrate escorting.
Written, automated or combined physical-access records are allowed; no universal retention duration is invented from the guide’s one-year example.
Identification, control and management include mechanical and electronic devices, locks and combinations; records alone are not treated as working access control.
Alternate-work safeguards must be defined and enforced; location-specific measures are permitted and VPN provision alone is not complete safeguarding.
Risk includes operations, assets and individuals, defined frequency, boundaries, likelihood/impact and dependencies; scanning is only an input, not the whole assessment.
Periodic and newly identified applicable-vulnerability triggers cover systems and applications; no universal weekly/monthly interval or scanner-brand mandate is invented.

findings.issue: Implied documented risk acceptance is never acceptable; the guide's example documents and tracks accepted risk.
findings.proposedText: Opening a ticket is not remediation. When the risk assessment supports deferring or accepting a vulnerability, document the reasoning, track the vulnerability and keep monitoring it; an undocumented or untracked acceptance does not show risk-based remediation.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 206 / printed 198 section; You document the reasoning behind accepting the risk of the unremediated flaws

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: You document the reasoning behind accepting the risk of the unremediated flaws

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Identification and risk-based remediation remain explicit; documented risk acceptance is not automatically remediation or permission for a CMMC deficiency. Guide discussion of deferred risks is not converted to blanket approval.
Defined periodic assessment checks effectiveness, with examination/interview/testing as possible methods; the annual question is accurately attributed to assessment considerations.
Identification, plan development and implementation remain distinct; operational plans are correctly distinguished from assessment POA&Ms and their 180-day rule.
Ongoing monitoring supports risk decisions and continued control effectiveness; continuous does not universally mean uninterrupted collection, and passive dashboards are insufficient without review.

System boundaries, operating environment, implementation, relationships, defined updates and non-applicable-designated-authority caveat are preserved; annual updates are attributed to the pinned Further Discussion.
External/key internal boundaries and monitoring/control/protection are all retained; an internet firewall or traffic logs alone do not fulfill all functions.
Identification and employment of architecture, development techniques and engineering principles are retained; feasible legacy-system application and lifecycle scope remain visible.

findings.issue: Separated the requirement from privileges, though the guide's stated intent is partly about accounts.
findings.proposedText: Review how user and management functionality are identified and physically or logically separated. The guide's stated intent includes keeping administration away from general users and having administrators administer only from their privileged accounts; separating staff duties is a different requirement.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 225 / printed 217 section; general users are not permitted to perform system administration functions

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: general users are not permitted to perform system administration functions

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Physical/logical separation of user and management functions is preserved and distinguished from staff duties and individual privileges; menu hiding is not separation.

findings.issue: Called it "not a generic file-sharing rule" though the guide's example counts folder isolation; left out one exclusion.
findings.proposedText: This is not a media-disposal requirement, and the discussion excludes deleted-data remnants, covert channels and components with only one user or role. The guide's example does count operating-system settings that stop users from reaching other users' folders, along with patches for processor flaws such as Meltdown and Spectre.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 227 / printed 219 section; the computer operating system is configured to prevent users from accessing other users

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: the computer operating system is configured to prevent users from accessing other users

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Shared-resource reuse, residual information and encrypted representations are addressed; deleted-data remnants and covert channels remain excluded as in the source Discussion.
Public components require physically/logically separated subnetworks; DMZ/cloud segmentation are examples and a different hostname alone is not adequate separation.
Deny-by-default/permit-by-exception covers inbound/outbound boundary and identified internal traffic; selective blocking on a default-allow policy is correctly distinguished.

findings.issue: The phrase in the prohibited arrangement is circular; it does not explain the two simultaneous network paths to a beginner.
findings.proposedText: When a remote device connects to the organization’s systems, prevent it from also reaching outside networks through a separate path. This is called split tunneling: one path reaches work systems while another bypasses that path to reach the internet or other outside resources.
findings.sourceSupport: PDF233/printed225 requirement/objective[a] and Discussion; PDF234/printed226 Further Discussion defines two connections: internal resources via VPN and simultaneous external-network access. Assessment consideration addresses communication outside that path with uncontrolled/unauthorized networks.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

findings.issue: The required connection arrangement is unnamed, so the example repeats the abstraction rather than demonstrating the source distinction.
findings.proposedText: At fictional Cedar Point Design, a remote-work laptop sends both company-system traffic and internet traffic through the company VPN while connected. The employee cannot change its settings to send internet traffic through a separate simultaneous path.
findings.sourceSupport: PDF234/printed226 Further Discussion and example describe disabling split tunneling and verifying all laptop traffic is routed through the VPN; PDF233/printed225 Discussion requires preventing settings from being readily configurable by users. This remains a fictional implementation example, not a universal VPN-product mandate.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

records.reviewNote: Technical/compliance fields accurately describe remote routing and overriding controls; Beginner meaning/example obscure the concept with circular arrangement wording and need a concrete two-path explanation.

findings.issue: Read as optional. The guide says the cryptography in this requirement protects CUI and "must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11" (FIPS-validated cryptography).
findings.proposedText: Map CUI transmission paths across internal and external networks and relevant devices. Identify the cryptographic mechanism or alternative physical safeguard that prevents disclosure. Where cryptography provides that protection, it must meet SC.L2-3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography).

records.reviewNote: Internal/external CUI transmission and cryptography/alternative physical safeguards are retained; an internal cable or one encrypted hop is not automatically complete protection.
Defined inactivity and session-end termination remain distinct from screen locking; no universal timeout is invented.
Establishment and ongoing key lifecycle management apply wherever cryptography is employed; manual methods remain possible and no universal rotation period is invented.

Validated module/version/deployment conditions are distinguished from an approved algorithm or marketing statement; confidentiality purpose and separate storage/transmission requirements remain explicit.
Remote activation prohibition and indication to present users are retained, including both dedicated-call-initiated conferencing and internet screen-sharing exclusions.
Mobile code means transferable executable code, not mobile-phone use; both control and monitoring are retained without mandating a universal JavaScript ban.

findings.issue: Could be read as monitoring call content; the requirement is about the use of VoIP technologies.
findings.proposedText: Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP), phone service carried over IP networks: who may use it, how it is set up, and whether unapproved VoIP tools or unauthorized uses appear.
findings.sourceSupport: CMMC Assessment Guide Level 2 v2.13, PDF 248 / printed 240 section; Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies

sourceCitation.quotedBasis: Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies

findings.resolution: Applied on 2026-10-15 after an AI-assisted comparison with the complete guide section; the earlier wording is in Git history. Human review pending.

records.reviewNote: Control and monitoring of VoIP are retained, but internet-based voice in Beginner meaning may imply public-internet-only scope; identify IP networks rather than that narrower label.
Session authenticity, peer confidence, ongoing communications, interception and hijacking are distinguished from encryption alone; a particular certificate mechanism is only an example.

findings.issue: Read as optional. The guide says the cryptography in this requirement protects CUI and "must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11" (FIPS-validated cryptography).
findings.proposedText: Identify where CUI is at rest and select mechanisms that protect its confidentiality. The guide discusses cryptographic and other protections; where cryptography protects CUI, it must meet SC.L2-3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography).

findings.issue: The second clause was hard to parse.
findings.proposedText: This wording does not mandate encryption as the only possible safeguard; conversely, encrypting storage does not replace limiting which accounts can read the CUI once it is unlocked.

records.reviewNote: At-rest state and confidentiality are retained; cryptographic and other adequate protections remain possible without a universal encryption-only mandate.
All identification/reporting/correction actions and their separately defined time expectations are retained; no universal patch deadline is invented.
Designated locations are identified and actual protection is provided; multiple protection approaches and custom-code detection limitations remain visible.
Response actions, monitored advisories and performed actions are distinct; sources and timing are not replaced with universal subscriptions or deadlines.
Available releases and successful protection updates remain distinct from merely scheduling a task; no guarantee of detecting every malicious function.

findings.issue: External-source scanning is present but neither example nor technical text names removable media. Make the guide’s explicitly assessed USB/CD scope clear rather than leaving learners to infer it from unfamiliar file routes.
findings.proposedText: Define periodic malicious-code scan frequency and enable real-time scanning of externally sourced files as they are downloaded, opened, or executed. Verify coverage and actual execution for files received through web or email routes and files copied from removable media such as USB drives.
findings.sourceSupport: PDF264/printed256 objective[c] covers files from external sources as downloaded, opened or executed. PDF265/printed257 Discussion includes portable storage; example includes files copied from USB drives; Potential Assessment Considerations explicitly asks whether USB/CD-ROM media are included and scanned.
findings.resolution: Applied after coordinating comparison of the cited complete guide section; associated objective mappings re-compared and preserved.

records.reviewNote: Periodic malicious-code scans and real-time external-file scans are both retained; explicitly name removable media in the technical scope to avoid an email/download-only interpretation.
Systems, inbound and outbound traffic all receive detection-oriented monitoring; no Level3 24/7 SOC obligation is imported into Level2.
Authorized use is defined and unauthorized use identified; authentication is distinguished from permission, and unusual activity requires interpretation rather than an automatic accusation.
